usage: subject with 이/가, default neutral framing
set phrase for cold easing off
examples: The weather is really nice today.
everyday small talk; 정말 adds warmth
Because it was cold I wore many layers.
weather as the 아서 reason clause
I wonder how the weather will be this weekend?
nuance: 날씨 is the pure-Korean word for the overall feel of the weather right now and is the single most common small-talk opener in Korea. Distinguish it from the Sino-Korean 기온(氣溫, 'air-temperature'), which is the measured number, and from 일기(日氣) / 기상(氣象), which are bookish words used in 일기예보 ('weather forecast'). You almost always pair 날씨 with the descriptive adjectives 좋다, 나쁘다, 춥다, 덥다, 맑다, 흐리다. The English-speaker pitfall is double: first, English says 'the weather IS cold' so learners reach for 이다, but Korean needs the adjective verb directly — 날씨가 추워요, never 날씨가 춥다이에요. Second, when stating a plain fact about the weather, default to the subject particle 가 (날씨가 좋아요), not the topic 는; 날씨는 좋아요 sounds like you are contrasting the weather against something else that is bad.

usage: I got caught in the rain
examples: Because it was raining I brought an umbrella.
nuance: Korean has no single verb meaning 'to rain'; instead precipitation 'arrives', so you say 비가 와요 (rain comes) using 오다. A more formal, written variant is 비가 내리다 ('rain falls'), favored in forecasts and lyrics, while 비가 오다 dominates everyday speech. To say rain stops, use the dedicated verb 그치다 (비가 그쳤어요), not 끝나다. Note 비 also forms many compounds: 소나기 (sudden shower), 장마 (the summer monsoon rains), 가랑비 (drizzle). The big English-speaker pitfall is inventing a verb: learners say 비가 해요 or 비해요 by analogy with English 'it rains', but 하다 never combines with 비 — the natural pairing is strictly 비가 오다 / 비가 내리다. A second trap is 비를 맞다 ('to take the rain on your body', i.e. get drenched), which uses 맞다, not 받다.

examples: It snows a lot in winter.
It is snowing and the wind is blowing too.
It snowed outside so the road is white.
nuance: 눈 means snow and, like rain, it 'comes': 눈이 와요 with 오다 (or the loftier 눈이 내리다). The crucial thing for English speakers is that 눈 is a perfect homograph and homophone with 눈 'eye' — only context tells them apart, and pitch differs subtly in some regions but spelling is identical, so 눈이 와요 in a weather chat can only mean snow. Snow-specific compounds are rich and culturally loaded: 첫눈 (the first snowfall of the season, tied to romance), 함박눈 (big fluffy flakes), 눈사람 (snowman), 눈싸움 (snowball fight). The pitfall, again, is reaching for a verb: never 눈이 해요; snow only pairs with 오다 or 내리다. Also resist forcing the English mass-noun logic — you don't 'do' snow or 'make it snow', you simply say it comes.

examples: The wind is blowing hard today.
It's cold because the wind is blowing.
In spring a warm wind blows.
nuance: 바람 is wind, and unlike rain or snow it does not 'come' — it 'blows', so the obligatory verb is 불다: 바람이 불어요. Describe its force with 세다 (강하다 in formal writing) and its pleasantness with 시원하다 or 선선하다. Watch a famous homonym trap: 바람 also means a romantic affair, as in 바람을 피우다 ('to cheat'), and 바람(이) 들다 can mean to be flighty; these are unrelated to weather but share the spelling, so context matters. The headline English-speaker pitfall is particle-verb mismatch: beginners copy the rain pattern and say 바람이 와요, but wind never takes 오다 — it is always 바람이 불다. A second subtle point: 'a strong wind' as a noun phrase is 센 바람 or 강한 바람, where the adjective comes before 바람, whereas to predicate it you say 바람이 세요.

usage: there are clouds in the sky
examples: The sky is really clear today.
There are many clouds in the sky.
The rain stopped and the sky turned blue.
nuance: 하늘 is the pure-Korean word for the physical sky, and by extension 'heaven' in religious or poetic contexts (하느님 'God' literally contains it). It is one of the headword + 에 nouns: because the sky is a static location where things merely exist, you say 하늘에 구름이 있어요, never 하늘에서, since 에서 marks a place where an action happens. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this 에 vs 에서 choice — 'a bird is flying IN the sky' becomes 하늘에서 새가 날아요 (action!), but 'there are clouds in the sky' stays 하늘에 (existence). A second trap is color: English keeps 'blue' fixed, but Korean 파랗다 is a ㅎ-irregular adjective, so 'the sky is blue' is 하늘이 파래요 (the ㅎ drops and a vowel shifts), not 파랗아요. Habitual collocations are 하늘이 맑다, 하늘이 흐리다, 하늘을 보다.

usage: there are clouds in the sky
examples: There are lots of clouds today.
There isn't a single cloud in the sky.
한 점도 + negative = not one bit
It's overcast because clouds have gathered.
nuance: 구름 is the pure-Korean word for cloud, counted in 점 ('구름 한 점' = one wisp of cloud) and habitually described with 많다 (plentiful) or the verb 끼다 ('to settle in / gather'), as in 구름이 끼다 — the standard way to say 'it clouds over'. The dramatic 먹구름 (literally 'ink cloud') means a dark storm cloud. Distinguish 구름 from 안개 (fog/mist), which sits at ground level, and from 흐리다, the adjective for an overcast sky (흐려요), not a noun. The classic English-speaker pitfall is copying the rain template and saying 구름이 와요 — clouds do not 'come' the way rain does; they 끼다, 몰려오다, or simply 많다. Another subtle error is treating 흐리다 as if it were the cloud itself; 'it's cloudy/overcast' is 날씨가 흐려요 or 구름이 꼈어요, two different structures.

examples: 마음에 들다 = to be to one's taste
nuance: 색 is the Sino-Korean root 色 ('color'), and it appears both as a standalone noun and, more often in casual speech, expanded to 색깔 — the two are interchangeable, with 색깔 feeling slightly warmer and more spoken. As a suffix, 색 attaches to color stems to make full color nouns: 빨간색, 파란색, 노란색. There is also a fixed set of bare Sino-Korean color words — 녹색(綠色) green, 황색(黃色) yellow, 흑색(黑色) black — used in formal or technical registers. The English-speaker pitfall is the object particle: 좋아하다 ('to like') takes a direct object, so 'I like this color' must be 이 색을 좋아해요, with 을, even though English 'like' feels stative. Note too that 좋아하다 expresses a held preference, whereas 마음에 들다 ('it pleases me') is for a fresh, in-the-moment liking of one specific thing.

Using 좋아하다 to react to one item you just saw; for an on-the-spot 'I like this one' Koreans prefer 이 색이 마음에 들어요.
Treating 색깔 as more formal than 색; it is actually the more casual, conversational form, while bare 색 and Sino words like 녹색 lean formal.

nuance: 빨간색 is built from the ㅎ-irregular adjective 빨갛다 ('to be red') plus 색, giving the noun 'the color red'. The key split for English speakers, who use one word 'red' for everything, is form-by-position: use the noun 빨간색 when red is the predicate or the thing you like (사과가 빨간색이에요 / 빨간색을 좋아해요), but use the bare modifier 빨간 directly before a noun (빨간 사과 'a red apple'). Saying 빨간색 사과 is understandable but sounds heavy and learner-ish; native speech contracts it to 빨간 사과. That modifier 빨간 comes from 빨갛다 → 빨간 (the ㅎ drops before the -ㄴ ending). Compare the slightly softer/duller 붉다 ('reddish, crimson'), more literary, as in 붉은 노을 'a red sunset'. Useful idiom: 새빨간 거짓말, literally a 'bright-red lie', means a barefaced lie.

examples: I gazed at the blue sky for a while.
I have lots of blue clothes.
nuance: 파란색 ('the color blue') comes from the ㅎ-irregular 파랗다, whose modifier form is 파란 — so 'a blue sky' is 파란 하늘, while 'the sky is blue' as a predicate is 하늘이 파래요 (adjective) or 하늘이 파란색이에요 (noun). A famous cultural pitfall hides here: Korean 파랗다/파란색 historically blankets both blue AND green for natural things, which is why a 'go' traffic light is 파란불 even though it looks green, and 푸르다 describes both 'blue sea' and 'green mountains/grass'. For a clearly leaf-green object, modern Korean uses 초록색 or 녹색(綠色). The English-speaker traps are therefore two: don't say 파란색 하늘 (drop 색 to get the natural 파란 하늘), and don't assume 파란 always equals English 'blue' — for grass or a traffic signal, 파란 can be what English calls green.

examples: In autumn yellow ginkgo leaves fall.
nuance: 노란색 ('yellow') is formed from the ㅎ-irregular adjective 노랗다, whose noun-modifier form is 노란: so 'a yellow flower' is 노란 꽃 and 'the flower is yellow' is 꽃이 노래요 or 꽃이 노란색이에요. Beware the most common spelling slip for English speakers: 노랑 is the bare color name (a noun, like English 'yellow' as a standalone word), but you cannot stick it straight onto a noun — '노랑 꽃' is wrong; before a noun you must use the adjective-derived 노란 꽃. There is also an expressive layer Korean loves: 노랗다 (yellow) vs 누렇다 (a darker, dingier yellow, like old paper or ripe rice), a brightness pair English flattens into one word. The Sino-Korean equivalent 황색(黃色) shows up in formal contexts such as 황색 신호 ('amber/yellow signal'). Habitual collocations: 노란 꽃, 노란 우산, 노란 머리(blond hair).

examples: It snowed in winter so the world is white.
The white snow is really pretty.
nuance: 하얀색 ('white') derives from the ㅎ-irregular adjective 하얗다, modifier form 하얀: so 'white snow' is 하얀 눈, while 'the snow is white' is 눈이 하얘요 or 눈이 하얀색이에요. Very common alongside it is 흰색, from the adjective 희다 — 흰 눈 / 흰색 셔츠 — which feels a touch more neutral and standard, whereas 하얀 carries a brighter, softer, almost cozy nuance; both are correct. Intensified, 새하얗다 → 새하얀 means dazzling pure-white. The English-speaker pitfalls: first, before a noun drop 색 and say 하얀 눈, not 하얀색 눈; second, the conjugation is irregular, so 'it is white' is 하얘요, never 하얗아요, and the modifier is 하얀, never 하얗은. Don't confuse this bright white with 회색(灰色) 'gray', a separate Sino-Korean color word.

structuredNuance.t: 하얀색 ('white') is the noun form. Intensified, 새하얗다 → 새하얀 means dazzling pure-white.

Very common alongside it is 흰색, from the adjective 희다 — 흰 눈 / 흰색 셔츠 — which feels a touch more neutral and standard, whereas 하얀 carries a brighter, softer, almost cozy nuance; both are correct. Don't confuse this bright white with 회색(灰色) 'gray', a separate Sino-Korean color word.
하얀색 derives from the ㅎ-irregular adjective 하얗다, modifier form 하얀: so 'white snow' is 하얀 눈, while 'the snow is white' is 눈이 하얘요 or 눈이 하얀색이에요.
The English-speaker pitfalls: first, before a noun drop 색 and say 하얀 눈, not 하얀색 눈; second, the conjugation is irregular, so 'it is white' is 하얘요, never 하얗아요, and the modifier is 하얀, never 하얗은.

mistakes: Writing 하얀색 눈 for 'white snow'; before a noun the natural phrase drops 색 to 하얀 눈 (or 흰 눈).
Conjugating it as 하얗아요; 하얗다 is ㅎ-irregular, so 'it is white' is 하얘요 and the modifier is 하얀.
Mixing up 하얀색 white and 회색 gray; they are different colors, 회색 being from 灰(ash)色.

examples: I want to buy a black car.
nuance: 검은색 ('black') comes from the adjective 검다, giving the modifier 검은 — so 'black clothes' is 검은 옷, while 'it is black' is 검어요 or 검은색이에요. A near-perfect synonym is 까만색 (from 까맣다, a ㅎ-irregular), which sounds a little more vivid and casual: 까만 머리 'black hair'. The intensified forms diverge — 새까만 (deep jet-black) is far more common than 시꺼먼, which can carry a grimy, dirty-black feeling. Unlike most colors here, 검다 is a regular adjective, so the modifier is straightforwardly 검은, not an irregular form. The Sino-Korean counterpart 흑색(黑色) and the loanword 블랙 appear in formal or fashion contexts. The English-speaker pitfall is the usual one: before a noun, native speech prefers 검은 옷 over the stiffer 검은색 옷, and 'I like black' needs the object particle — 검은색을 좋아해요, not 검은색 좋아해요.
